items.title: Cognition Without Consciousness: A Minimal Conceptual Framework for Understanding LLMs and Human Cognitive Evolution
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made visible a long‑standing philosophical tension: sophisticated symbolic cognition can arise from large‑scale pattern extraction even in the absence of consciousness. This observation motivates a minimalist conceptual framework grounded in an ontological distinction between conscious regulation and symbolic structures. Language is treated as a crystallized form of human cognition—an externalized, culturally accumulated substrate created by conscious agents over millennia—while the human brain is understood as a biological system that evolved to operate over this symbolic layer. Within this view, consciousness and symbolic cognition are not different degrees of the same process but distinct kinds of cognitive organization: consciousness generates, grounds, and regulates symbols, whereas symbolic cognition manipulates them.LLMs illuminate this asymmetry by reproducing symbolic reasoning without conscious access, motivation, or subjective experience. Their performance therefore raises epistemological questions about the nature of meaning, grounding, and cognitive stability. The proposed framework situates these questions within a broader account of human cognitive evolution shaped by gene–culture coevolution and the emergence of culturally scaffolded symbolic systems. Finally, the article introduces an information‑theoretic constraint (the AI Theorem) suggesting that purely computational systems inevitably accumulate drift in the absence of a regulatory layer, offering a philosophical explanation for why artificial cognition may remain structurally distinct from biological minds.

items.title: Comparative analysis of cervical spine pain and mobility in car versus motorbike drivers: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Cervical spine pain, particularly among car and motorbike drivers, is a common musculoskeletal issue due to prolonged static postures and repetitive neck movements. This study investigates the prevalence and correlation between cervical spine pain and mobility in car and motorbike drivers. Methods In this cross-sectional study, conducted at Integral Hospital and Research Centre, India, 100 participants (50 car drivers and 50 motorbike drivers) were randomly selected with individuals reporting cervical pain. Participants completed demographic information, driving duration, and cervical pain severity and underwent cervical mobility assessments using smartphone-based tools. Statistical analysis was conducted using independent t-tests and Pearson’s correlation with 95% confidence intervals and Cohen’s d effect sizes, at a significance level of p ≤ 0.05. Results Car drivers (mean age 39.2, driving experience 15.6 years, 70% male) and motorbike drivers (mean age 34.8, experience 12.4 years, 80% male) were studied. Motorbike drivers reported higher cervical pain on visual analogue scale (VAS) 5 compared to car drivers VAS 4. Inverse correlations between cervical pain and mobility were noted, with motorbike drivers showing significantly lower cervical mobility across all movements. Negative correlations varied in strength across different movements for both groups, generally more substantial for car drivers. Conclusion This study highlights the association between cervical pain and reduced mobility among drivers, particularly motorbike drivers. Although causality cannot be determined, the findings support ergonomic interventions and driver education to promote better postures and musculoskeletal health.

items.title: Coping Strategies and Trauma-Informed Interventions for Residential Support Workers: We Lean on Each Other
items.abstract: Abstract Despite growing attention to trauma-informed care for young people, the experiences and support needs of Residential Support Workers (RSWs) remain underexplored. This study examines how RSWs build and maintain support networks in response to workplace trauma and identifies locally grounded interventions that workers perceive as necessary for their wellbeing and professional sustainability. A qualitative design was employed, drawing on data from 20 semi-structured interviews and five focus group discussions with RSWs. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, following a six-phase approach. Findings indicate that informal peer support networks serve as the primary and most trusted source of emotional and practical support, often compensating for inconsistent formal systems. Reflective supervision was experienced as uneven and manager-dependent, while safety - particularly staffing levels, consistency, and organisational responses to critical incidents - emerged as foundational to worker wellbeing. Experiences of trauma were further shaped by race and cultural identity, highlighting the need for culturally responsive, localized interventions. The study offers practice-relevant insights into trauma-informed support for RSWs and suggests the development of worker-centred intervention models.

items.title: COVID-19-induced psychological distress and sexual quality of life of healthcare workers: a global scoping review
items.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic had substantial physical, emotional, and psychological effects on healthcare workers. Although its mental health impact has been extensively researched, little is known about its effects on sexual health. Despite its importance to psychological resilience and professional functioning, sexual health remains underexplored in occupational health research. This scoping review synthesises evidence on the impact of COVID-19-induced psychological distress on the sexual quality of life of healthcare workers and its implications for professional performance and care delivery. Following the JBI scoping review framework, databases including MEDLINE, SCOPUS, Cochrane CENTRAL, JSTOR, Dimensions AI, WHO IRIS, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, Google, and Google Scholar were searched. Eighteen studies published between 2020 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Sexual dysfunction prevalence ranged from 35% to over 80%, affecting desire, arousal, satisfaction, and orgasm. These outcomes were associated with anxiety, depression, and PTSD, and were exacerbated by long shifts, frontline assignments, partner separation, and fear of infection. Sociodemographic factors also influenced outcomes. Limited evidence linked sexual dysfunction to burnout, emotional exhaustion, and reduced care quality, while interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy showed modest benefits. Addressing sexual health is essential for improving both well-being and professional functioning among healthcare workers.

items.title: Cyberwarfare and the Future of Global Conflict
items.abstract: In an era where digital technology dictates the rhythm of modern society, warfare has transcended physical battlegrounds and entered a domain where lines are blurred, and combatants remain unseen. This book delves into the profound implications of cyberwarfare on the future of global conflicts, unraveling the intricacies of digital battles that shape political power struggles and redefine national security. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, presents an analytical exploration of how cyberwarfare has evolved from a strategic tool to an indispensable instrument of modern military doctrine. He examines the ethical, philosophical, and geopolitical dilemmas surrounding this form of warfare, raising critical questions about sovereignty, responsibility, and the potential catastrophic consequences of digital escalation. Published in 2011, this work is an essential read for policymakers, scholars, and individuals seeking to understand how the silent war of codes and algorithms is sculpting the future of international relations and power dynamics. The rapid advancement of digital technology has revolutionized military strategies and international conflicts. Cyberwarfare has become an integral component of statecraft, influencing national defense policies and global security. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explores how nations increasingly depend on digital infrastructure and how vulnerabilities in these systems present new challenges in conflict prevention and resolution. Published in 2011, this book offers a critical examination of the historical trajectory and future implications of cyberwarfare. The nature of warfare has fundamentally shifted with the advent of digital technology. This book defines cyberwarfare as the use of digital attacks to disrupt, sabotage, or compromise a nation’s military, political, or economic systems. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, elaborates on key principles such as cyber espionage, cyber deterrence, and digital sovereignty. With the increasing digitization of society, cyberattacks have become a tool for both state and non-state actors. From hacking government databases to disabling critical infrastructure, these operations demonstrate the potential for large-scale disruption. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, highlights significant cases that illustrate the growing reliance on digital warfare and the consequences for global stability. Cyberwarfare operates on principles distinct from conventional warfare. Unlike traditional military conflicts, cyber operations occur in an invisible domain where anonymity and deniability provide strategic advantages. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, dissects the methodologies used in cyberattacks, from malware deployment to artificial intelligence-enhanced cyber operations. Identifying cyberwarfare involves analyzing patterns of attacks, technological advancements, and geopolitical tensions. The book explores how nations prepare for digital conflicts, investing in cybersecurity, counterintelligence, and cyber defense mechanisms. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, provides insight into the signs that indicate an ongoing or imminent cyberwar. Understanding cyberwarfare requires analyzing the factors that shape its execution. From technological capabilities to political will, multiple elements contribute to the effectiveness of digital warfare. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explores how artificial intelligence, big data, and machine learning are integrated into cyber strategies. Several factors influence the effectiveness of cyberwarfare, including national cybersecurity policies, international regulations, and the ethical considerations of digital warfare. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, evaluates the key determinants that dictate how cyber conflicts unfold and their long-term consequences. Cyberwarfare is executed through a combination of offensive and defensive strategies. Countries invest in cyber intelligence, surveillance, and countermeasures to mitigate threats. This book presents a comprehensive analysis of cyber defense frameworks and offensive digital tactics, as examined by Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA. The rise of cyberwarfare presents numerous challenges, from regulatory loopholes to ethical dilemmas. While some nations advocate for cyber arms control, others engage in cyber conflicts without accountability. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, assesses the geopolitical complexities that define the digital battlefield. The future of warfare will be increasingly shaped by cyber capabilities, where battles are fought through algorithms rather than bullets. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, concludes by emphasizing the urgent need for global cooperation in establishing norms and frameworks to manage the risks associated with cyber conflicts.

items.title: Detecting HIV-Related Stigma in Clinical Narratives Using Large Language Models
items.abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related stigma is a critical psychosocial determinant of health for people living with HIV (PLWH), influencing mental health, engagement in care, and treatment outcomes. Although stigma-related experiences are documented in clinical narratives, there is a lack of off-the-shelf tools to extract and categorize them. This study aims to develop a large language model (LLM)-based tool for identifying HIV stigma from clinical notes. We identified clinical notes from PLWH receiving care at the University of Florida (UF) Health between 2012 and 2022. Candidate sentences were identified using expert-curated stigma-related keywords and iteratively expanded via clinical word embeddings. A total of 1,332 sentences were manually annotated across four stigma subscales: Concern with Public Attitudes, Disclosure Concerns, Negative Self-Image, and Personalized Stigma. We compared GatorTron-large and BERT as encoder-based baselines, and GPT-OSS-20B, LLaMA-8B, and MedGemma-27B as generative LLMs, under zero-shot and few-shot prompting. GatorTron-large achieved the best overall performance (Micro F1 = 0.62). Few-shot prompting substantially improved generative model performance, with 5-shot GPT-OSS-20B and LLaMA-8B achieving Micro-F1 scores of 0.57 and 0.59, respectively. Performance varied by stigma subscale, with Negative Self-Image showing the highest predictability and Personalized Stigma remaining the most challenging. Zero-shot generative inference exhibited non-trivial failure rates (up to 32%). This study develops the first practical NLP tool for identifying HIV stigma in clinical notes.
